paraphrase: Atharvan tells Śāṇḍilya: there are eight limbs — ten yamas, ten niyamas, eight postures, three prāṇāyāmas, five pratyāhāras, dhāraṇā, two kinds of dhyāna and one samādhi.

paraphrase: Non-injury is causing no pain to any being by mind, speech or body; truth is speaking what is true and beneficial; … purity is external (earth and water) and internal (by knowledge of the Self).

paraphrase: Five pratyāhāras: forcibly withdrawing the senses; seeing all as the Self; renouncing the fruits of daily acts; turning from all objects; and holding (the breath) at the eighteen vital points in ascending and descending order.

paraphrase: Dhāraṇā is threefold (fixing mind in the Self, outer space in the heart-space, the five deities in the elements); dhyāna is with qualities (form) or without (the Self's nature); samādhi is the union of jīvātman and paramātman free from the triad.

paraphrase: Śāṇḍilya, not finding brahmavidyā in the four Vedas, asks Atharvan; Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite, and 'that you are'.

paraphrase: Brahman has three forms — with parts, without parts, and with-and-without parts; its most manifest form is Dattātreya, who gave himself to Atri and was born of Anasūyā; his meditation form is the naked avadhūta smeared with ash.

checks.note: E-text ch. 3 gives the three forms of Brahman (sakala, niṣkala, sakalaniṣkala) and derives the name Dattātreya (datta, son of Atri and Anasūyā).
